description: Teacher-approved OCR J277 five-lesson You Do pilot

questions.text: Explain why binary search requires the array to be sorted before searching.

scheme.point: The array must be in a known sorted order.
The comparison with the middle element then determines which half can safely be discarded.

questions.note: Saying “because it is faster” alone is insufficient.

questions.text: A sorted array has the values [2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 21, 27]. Show the steps of binary search for 21 using zero-based indices and midpoint = (low + high) DIV 2. Record the first midpoint, the updated search range and the midpoint at which 21 is found.

scheme.point: First midpoint index 3, value 12.
Since 21 > 12, update low to 4 (search indices 4–6).
New midpoint index 5, value 21; found at index 5.

questions.note: Accept a clear trace table or equivalent ordered steps.

questions.text: A sorted array has the values [3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23, 27, 31, 35]. Show the steps of binary search for 8, starting with low = 0 and high = 8. Use midpoint = (low + high) DIV 2 and show the midpoint values checked. State the condition that ends the unsuccessful search.

scheme.point: mid = 4; value 19; set high = 3.
mid = 1; value 7; set low = 2.
mid = 2; value 11; set high = 1.
low (2) > high (1), so the target is absent and the search ends.

questions.note: Zero-based indexing and integer division. Do not award a final index for an absent target.

questions.text: State two environmental impacts of frequently replacing working school laptops.

scheme.point: Electronic waste from discarded devices.
Use of energy/raw materials and resulting emissions during manufacture.

questions.note: Also accept other distinct valid environmental impacts; do not credit repeats.

questions.text: A school uses an online-only parent communication app. Explain one way this could disadvantage some families and one practical step the school could take to reduce that problem.

scheme.point: Identify the disadvantage: some families have poor connectivity, lack devices or need accessible alternatives.
Explain how that prevents timely access to homework, attendance messages or school information.
Give a relevant mitigation, such as printed letters, phone calls, translation or accessible formats.

questions.note: Any coherent supported disadvantage and matched response can earn full marks.

questions.text: A multi-academy trust plans to replace printed letters with a compulsory online-only system for homework, attendance and communication with parents. Discuss the ethical, cultural and environmental implications of this proposal. You should consider different viewpoints and reach a supported conclusion.

scheme.point: No relevant response.
Limited relevant knowledge; simple or unconnected points, little application to the trust.
Some developed discussion of benefits and drawbacks linked to the scenario; partial balance and a basic judgement.
Well-developed, balanced argument addressing ethical/cultural and environmental implications, applied to the trust; clear reasoned conclusion.

indicative: Advantages: faster communication, accessible records and potentially less printing, delivery and paper waste.
Ethical/cultural concerns: digital exclusion, accessibility needs, language barriers, privacy of pupil/family data, unequal access.
Environmental trade-offs: reduced paper/travel versus electricity, devices, manufacturing emissions and electronic waste.
Reasoned decision: adopt digital by default but preserve accessible paper, telephone or translated routes and protect personal data.
questions.note: Teacher-generated indicative levels, not copied from OCR’s official mark scheme. Assess the whole response; do not add one mark per bullet.

questions.text: State what is meant by input and output in a computer program.

scheme.point: Input: data received by a program, for example entered by a user.
Output: information produced by the program, for example displayed on screen.

questions.note: Two distinct definitions: do not award two marks for examples alone.

questions.text: A cinema sells tickets for £6 each. A customer chooses how many tickets to buy. Describe how input, processing and output would be used to display the total cost.

scheme.point: Input: obtain the number of tickets from the customer.
Processing: multiply the number by £6 to calculate the total.
Output: display the calculated total to the customer.

questions.note: Accept equivalent wording tied to the stated ticket scenario.

questions.text: Tickets for a school concert cost £6 each. Write OCR Exam Reference Language instructions to assign the ticket price, input the number of tickets as an integer, calculate the total cost and print the total.

scheme.point: Correct assignment of price: ticketPrice = 6.
An integer input is stored: tickets = int(input("Number of tickets?"))
Total is calculated by multiplication: total = ticketPrice * tickets.
The total is output: print(total).

questions.model_code:
ticketPrice = 6
tickets = int(input("Number of tickets?"))
total = ticketPrice * tickets
print(total)
questions.note: An equivalent OCR ERL solution with valid variable names earns the same marks. Do not deduct for harmless prompt wording.

questions.text: A school represents pupil records in a two-dimensional array. State what a row and a column represent in this table.

scheme.point: Each row represents one pupil (one record).
Each column represents one field, e.g. name or tutor group.

questions.note: OCR J277 explicitly permits 2D arrays to emulate records and data tables.

questions.text: A school stores pupil names and tutor groups in a two-dimensional array called pupils. Explain how rows, columns and indices could be used to find the tutor group for a particular pupil.

scheme.point: A row represents a particular pupil.
A column represents the field required, here the tutor group.
Use the chosen row and column indices to access that value, e.g. pupils[1,1].

questions.note: Assume zero-based indices and column 1 = tutor group, as shown in Code First.

questions.text: A school uses a two-dimensional array where column 0 stores a pupil name and column 1 stores the tutor group. Write OCR Exam Reference Language statements to declare an array with two rows and two columns, store "Ben" and "10B" in the second row, then print that pupil’s tutor group.

scheme.point: array pupils[2,2] declared.
pupils[1,0] = "Ben" sets the second pupil name.
pupils[1,1] = "10B" sets the tutor group.
print(pupils[1,1]) prints the correct indexed field.

questions.note: OCR ERL only; a 2D array emulates the record fields.

096.title: Primary Storage: RAM, ROM and Cache

questions.text: State which of RAM and ROM is volatile and which is non-volatile.

scheme.point: RAM is volatile.
ROM is non-volatile.

questions.text: A pupil uses several applications on a laptop. Explain how cache memory can help the CPU run programs efficiently.

scheme.point: Cache holds frequently or recently used data and instructions.
The CPU can retrieve these more quickly than from main RAM.
This reduces waiting for memory access and may improve overall performance.

questions.note: Avoid claiming that cache makes every program automatically faster.

questions.text: A school is choosing between two otherwise identical laptops. Laptop A has 4 GB RAM; Laptop B has 8 GB RAM. Pupils regularly run applications that together need about 6 GB of working memory. Justify which laptop is more suitable, including one limitation of upgrading RAM alone.

scheme.point: Select Laptop B (8 GB).
Explain that 8 GB can accommodate the stated 6 GB working-memory demand.
Laptop A may rely more heavily on virtual memory, which is slower than RAM.
Acknowledge that CPU/storage or other bottlenecks can still limit performance despite extra RAM.

questions.note: Accept equivalent technically accurate justifications. The scenario fixes other specifications to isolate RAM.
